senses.sense_definition: Either of the two times each year (in March and September) when the sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are of approximately equal length.

examples.text: The spring <w>equinox</w> usually occurs on or around March twentieth in the northern hemisphere.
Many cultures celebrate the autumn <w>equinox</w> with harvest festivals and traditional feasts.

senses.sense_definition: Either of the two points on the celestial sphere where the ecliptic intersects the celestial equator.

examples.text: Astronomers use the celestial <w>equinox</w> as a reference point for measuring coordinates in the sky.
The position of each <w>equinox</w> slowly shifts over thousands of years due to precession.

senses.sense_definition: The condition of day and night being of equal duration; an equality of light and darkness.

examples.text: Poets often compare emotional balance to an <w>equinox</w> between joy and sorrow.
During that rare period, the daylight and dark remained in perfect <w>equinox</w> across the globe.

senses.sense_definition: A strong gale traditionally believed to occur regularly around the time of an equinox.

examples.text: Sailors braced their ship against the fierce <w>equinox</w> that battered the coastline.
The sudden <w>equinox</w> blew violently across the harbor, tearing loose several small fishing boats.

senses.sense_definition: The celestial equator or the terrestrial equator.

examples.text: Old navigation logs recorded the exact latitude as the vessel sailed north of the <w>equinox</w>.
Early cartographers sometimes designated the Earth's central line simply as the <w>equinox</w>.

traits.comment: archaic term for the equator or celestial equator
